title: High-Stakes Testing — Ethics and Validity

pts: A high-stakes test has significant real-world consequences for the test-taker — university admission, immigration status, employment eligibility.
This raises the ethical bar considerably beyond a classroom quiz, where consequences are largely confined to formative feedback.
This connects directly to Unit 21's test-quality framework, now considered alongside genuinely higher ethical stakes.

v: A list of tests your learners take

items: List every English test your learners take in a year, from class quizzes to board and entrance examinations.
For each, note who uses the score and what decision it informs.
Place each test on a line from ‘low stakes’ to ‘high stakes’.
For the three highest-stakes tests, list the consequences of a low score.
Discuss how the ethical demands on each test change along the line.
DIET faculty run the task with trainee teachers, adding tests the trainees themselves took.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A partial map (written for this book):

lines: Weekly spelling quiz → teacher → which words to revise → low stakes.
Class 10 board English paper → board, colleges → stream and college admission → high stakes.
An international English proficiency test → universities, employers, immigration authorities → study abroad, work visa → very high stakes.

blocks.x: A classroom quiz with a poorly worded item wastes ten minutes; a high-stakes test with the same flaw may change a life. Unit 21’s quality framework applies to both, but the ethical bar rises with the stakes.

body: Purpose: to show rising consequences. Content: a line of tests from a small quiz sheet on the left to a large examination hall on the right; above it, weights of increasing size labelled with consequences (‘revise words’, ‘choose stream’, ‘visa’). Style: clean infographic. Board version: a line with labelled points.

items: Google Sheets (free) to tabulate tests, users and decisions.

blocks.x: A three-column table on chart paper.

pts: Consequential validity asks not just whether a test measures what it claims to, but what the real-world consequences of its use actually are.
A technically valid test can still produce unjust consequences if used in ways its original validation didn't anticipate or support.
This extends Unit 21's validity discussion into ethically, not just technically, contested territory.
points.who: Samuel Messick's work on consequential validity

v: A case study of a test used for a new purpose

items: Read a short case in which a test designed for one purpose is used for another.
Ask Messick’s questions: does the score support this interpretation? Is it appropriate for this decision? What are the consequences, intended and unintended?
List who benefits and who might be harmed.
Suggest what additional evidence a responsible user would need.
Consider a use of an English test in your own district.
Groups take different stakeholder roles (learner, parent, employer, test designer) and argue from that role.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A district uses a Class 8 English reading test, designed to diagnose reading needs, to rank schools and publish the results. Teachers begin to coach test formats; weaker readers are discouraged from attending on test day.
Interpretation: the scores show reading levels, not school quality.
Unintended consequences: narrowed teaching; exclusion of weaker learners.
Needed: evidence that school rankings reflect teaching rather than intake.

blocks.x: The test is technically sound for its original purpose. The problem lies in its use.

body: Purpose: to show consequential validity. Content: a test paper at the centre, arrows running out to people and outcomes (a learner, a school gate, a newspaper ranking), some green (intended), some red (unintended), with labels as well as colours. Style: clear network diagram. Board version: a box with arrows and labels.

items: None needed; this is a case discussion.

pts: A test can systematically disadvantage certain groups through culturally-specific content, unfamiliar item formats, or norms reflecting one dominant variety.
This connects directly to Unit 59's critical language awareness — standard-variety assumptions embedded in tests are an equity question, not just a technical one.
Bias analysis, comparing performance patterns across different learner groups, is a genuine technical safeguard worth understanding even for non-specialists.

items: Work in pairs through a past English paper, item by item.
For each item, ask: does it require cultural knowledge unrelated to English (for example, a winter sport or an urban lifestyle)?
Ask whether any item format would be unfamiliar to some learners (for example, computer-based formats for learners who rarely use computers).
Ask whether answers in a legitimate Indian English usage would be marked wrong (Unit 74).
Record flagged items and suggest revisions.
Where results are available, compare the performance of two groups of learners, such as rural and urban, on each item; a large difference on one item may signal bias.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Reading passage on a ski holiday in the Alps. Cultural knowledge may help some learners guess answers. Revision: a trek in Himachal Pradesh.
Vocabulary item: ‘The opposite of “lift” is…’ Assumes one variety’s usage; ‘elevator’ or ‘lift’ are both standard.
Item: ‘Correct the sentence: “I am having two brothers.”’ A usage heard widely in Indian English; the test must decide which norm it assesses, and say so openly.

blocks.x: Statistical methods such as differential item functioning check whether learners of equal ability from different groups do differently on an item. Teachers need not calculate it, but should know that the idea exists. Standard-language assumptions in tests are an equity question as well as a technical one (Unit 59).

body: Purpose: to show how one item can be easy for some and hard for others for reasons unrelated to English. Content: two learners reading the same question about skiing; one has a thought bubble with a ski resort, the other a question mark. Style: gentle. Board version: two faces and one question.

items: Google Sheets (free) to compare item scores across groups.

blocks.x: A paper checklist of bias questions attached to each paper under review.

body: The ILTA Code of Ethics sets out principles for language testers, including respect for the dignity of test-takers, confidentiality, and a responsibility to consider the effects of tests on society (ILTA 2000). It is freely available on the association’s website [VERIFY current URL].

points.sub: Who can even sit the exam
pts: Cost, location, accommodation availability, and language of test administration all affect who can access a given high-stakes test at all.
This connects to Unit 23's inclusive-teaching principles, extended to formal, high-stakes assessment contexts specifically.
Accommodations for learners with additional needs (Unit 23) are both a fairness and, in many contexts, a legal requirement.

v: Information on registration for one high-stakes test

items: Choose one high-stakes test your learners may take.
Find its fee, the nearest centre, the modes (paper or computer), the language of instructions and the accommodations available.
Imagine three learners: a girl in a village 80 km from the centre, a learner with a visual impairment, a learner whose family earns daily wages.
List the barriers each faces before the test begins.
Identify one barrier the school could help reduce.
Invite a parent or former student to describe their experience of registering and travelling for a test.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Barriers for three learners (written for this book):

lines: Girl in a village: travel the day before; overnight stay; family concern for safety.
Learner with visual impairment: needs a scribe or enlarged paper; application must be made early with a disability certificate.
Daily-wage family: fee equals several days’ earnings; no money for practice materials.

blocks.x: School response: hold an information session each year on accommodations and application deadlines, and help with forms. Inclusive assessment (Unit 23) is not only good practice; in India, accommodations for candidates with disabilities are a legal right (Government of India 2016).

body: Purpose: to show access barriers. Content: three roads leading to an examination hall; one smooth, one with a long distance marker, one with a toll gate and a step without a ramp. Style: simple, map-like. Board version: three lines with obstacles drawn on them.

items: Official test websites (free to consult) for fees and accommodation policies [VERIFY current details before publication].

blocks.x: A printed information sheet on accommodations for the school notice board.

pts: High-stakes language tests function as genuine gatekeepers to migration, education and employment for many test-takers worldwide.
This connects to Unit 59's discussion of English as a gatekeeper more broadly — testing is where that gatekeeping becomes formally institutionalised.
Teachers preparing learners for such tests carry real responsibility, given these genuine, significant stakes.

v: Short testimonies (written for this book); discussion questions

items: Learners read three short fictional testimonies from people whose lives were shaped by an English test result.
In groups, they identify what the test controlled access to and whether the test seemed a fair measure for that purpose.
They discuss: should an English test decide this? What else could?
Each group writes a 150-word opinion paragraph using hedging language (Unit 61).
Share and compare positions.
Hold a structured debate (Unit 39): ‘English tests are a fair way to decide university admission’.
Support: provide an opinion-paragraph frame and a hedging bank (It could be argued that… This may…).
Challenge: learners research how two countries use English tests for migration and compare.

lines: Anitha is a skilled nurse from Kerala. She needs a minimum band score to work abroad. She has passed three times in reading and listening but missed the writing score by half a band twice. Each attempt costs her a month’s salary.
It could be argued that nurses must write clear reports, so a writing test is reasonable. However, a general academic essay may not measure the writing nurses actually do.

blocks.x: English is often a gatekeeper to opportunity (Unit 59). High-stakes tests are where that gatekeeping becomes formal and institutional.

body: Purpose: to show tests as gatekeepers. Content: a tall gate with a lock shaped like a test paper; on the far side, a university, a hospital and an aeroplane; people waiting on the near side, some holding keys. Style: symbolic, restrained. Board version: a gate with three labels beyond it.

items: None needed; this is a reading and discussion task.

pts: The commercial test-preparation industry creates its own ethical questions — access inequality between learners who can and can't afford intensive preparation.
This connects to Unit 66's exam-preparation ethics, extended to the broader commercial and access context surrounding high-stakes testing.
Awareness of this dimension doesn't necessarily change individual teaching practice, but informs a fuller professional understanding of the field.

v: Advertisements or brochures from test-preparation providers

items: Collect three test-preparation advertisements (online or from local newspapers).
List their claims (e.g. ‘guaranteed band 7’) and the cost.
Discuss who can afford this help and who cannot.
Consider what the school could offer free: familiarization with formats, practice under timed conditions, feedback on writing.
Agree a school statement on ethical exam preparation (Unit 66).
Survey older learners (anonymously) about how many attend paid coaching and why.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Claims: ‘Crack the test in 15 days’, ‘Guaranteed score’. No test preparation can honestly guarantee a score.
Equity: a learner who pays for intensive coaching gets repeated practice and feedback; a learner who cannot, does not.
School response: two free familiarization workshops a year, and a bank of practice materials in the library.

blocks.x: Awareness of the industry does not necessarily change what happens in your own lessons, but it gives you a fuller understanding of why some learners arrive better prepared than others.

body: Purpose: to show unequal preparation. Content: two runners on a track, one with a coach and training equipment, one alone in ordinary shoes; the same finish line labelled ‘test day’. Style: clear, non-judgemental. Board version: two stick figures on a line.

items: Free official sample tests on test providers’ websites [VERIFY availability].

blocks.x: Printed sample papers kept in the school library.

pts: Teachers and institutions can advocate for fairer assessment practices — accommodation policies, bias review, transparent scoring criteria — within their sphere of influence.
This connects to Unit 46's transparency principle, extended from classroom rubrics to institutional and high-stakes testing advocacy.
Even without individual power to redesign a major exam, informed critical awareness supports better-informed professional advocacy.

v: A school or district assessment policy

items: Draw three circles: my classroom, my school, beyond the school (district, board).
In each circle, list one change towards fairer assessment that you could propose, such as transparent rubrics (Unit 46), an accommodations checklist, or a bias review of internal papers.
For each, name who decides and what evidence would persuade them.
Choose one proposal and draft a short, respectful note to the decision-maker.
Share drafts and improve them.
A DIET or cluster resource centre compiles proposals from several schools for the district.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A draft note (written for this book):

lines: To the Head Teacher: Last term, three learners with dyslexia did not receive extra time in our internal English examination because the request came too late. I propose that class teachers identify such learners in June and that we publish the accommodation procedure on the notice board. I am happy to prepare the list and the notice.

blocks.x: Even without power to redesign a board examination, informed teachers can improve the tests they do control and raise questions about the ones they do not.

body: Purpose: to show where teachers can act. Content: three concentric circles labelled ‘Classroom’, ‘School’, ‘Beyond’, with small icons for proposals in each (a rubric, a notice board, a letter). Style: clean. Board version: three circles with labels.

items: Google Docs (free) for drafting and sharing proposals.

blocks.x: A handwritten note and a copy for the staff file.

pts: High-stakes testing serves genuine, necessary gatekeeping and quality-assurance functions in education and employment, even amid these real ethical complexities.
The realistic professional stance is critical awareness and advocacy for improvement, not wholesale rejection of assessment's legitimate role.
This mirrors Unit 59's balanced critical stance — informed, reflective practice within genuine, real-world constraints.

items: List the legitimate functions of high-stakes tests (fair selection, common standards, quality assurance).
List the ethical risks identified in this unit.
In pairs, write a five-sentence professional position that acknowledges both.
Test it against a case from point 2 or point 5: does it help you decide what to do?
Keep it with your teaching philosophy (Unit 25).
Trainee teachers compare their positions at the start and end of an assessment module.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: High-stakes tests are necessary: without them, selection may depend on connections or wealth. But no test is neutral. I will prepare learners honestly, without false promises. I will check my own tests for bias and access. I will speak up, respectfully and with evidence, when a test is used in ways it was not designed for.

blocks.x: This mirrors the balanced critical stance of Unit 59: critical awareness and advocacy, not wholesale rejection. Part IV takes the discussion further with major international tests in Unit 92 and the ethics of AI scoring in Unit 99.

body: Purpose: to show a balanced stance. Content: a balance scale with ‘fair selection, common standards’ on one pan and ‘bias, access, misuse’ on the other; a teacher’s hand adding a weight labelled ‘informed advocacy’. Style: calm, balanced. Board version: a scale with labels.

items: None needed; this is a reflection task.

body: Take the last internal English paper you set. Review it with a colleague using the bias questions in point 3 and the access questions in point 4. Revise one item and one procedure before the next examination.

dek: Unit 73 of 100: assessment with real, significant consequences for learners' lives demands ethical scrutiny beyond the technical validity and reliability of Unit 21.

aims.x: Unit 21 introduced validity, reliability and practicality as the qualities of a good classroom test. This unit asks what changes when a test decides a learner’s future: a place at university, a job, a visa, a scholarship. At that point the technical questions remain, but ethical questions join them. Who is advantaged by this test? Who is excluded before they even sit it? What happens to people because of the scores? The unit is for experienced teachers, exam coordinators and teacher educators.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what makes a test high-stakes;
explain consequential validity and why it widens the idea of validity;
identify possible sources of bias in test content, format and norms;
analyse who can and cannot access a test, and what accommodations exist;
describe how language tests act as gatekeepers;
discuss the ethics of the commercial test-preparation industry;
advocate for fairer assessment within your own sphere of influence;
take a balanced, critically informed stance on high-stakes testing.

why: Why this matters. A test can be technically well-designed and still raise serious ethical questions about who it advantages, who it excludes, and what its real-world consequences are.

background.x: For most of the twentieth century, validity meant a test’s accuracy: does it measure what it claims to measure? Samuel Messick (1989) argued for a unified view in which validity concerns the interpretations and uses of scores, including their social consequences. A test may measure reading well, yet using its scores to decide who may train as a nurse raises further questions: is reading the right thing to measure for that decision, and what happens to those who fail? Lyle Bachman and Adrian Palmer (2010) built this into an assessment use argument, in which test developers must justify each step from performance to decision to consequence.

Elana Shohamy (2001) drew attention to the power of tests. Because tests carry authority, they can shape curricula, define what counts as knowledge and control access to opportunities, often in ways their designers never intended. Tim McNamara and Carsten Roever (2006) examined the social dimension of language testing, including the use of tests in citizenship and migration decisions. Liz Hamp-Lyons (1997) linked washback (Unit 57) to ethical responsibility. The International Language Testing Association adopted a Code of Ethics setting out testers’ responsibilities to test-takers and society (ILTA 2000).

In India, board examinations, entrance examinations and recruitment tests function as high-stakes gates for millions of learners every year, and English is often a significant factor. NEP 2020 calls for board examinations that test core capacities rather than rote learning and that reduce the need for coaching, and proposes a national assessment centre, PARAKH, to set norms and standards (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 makes reasonable accommodation, such as scribes and extra time, a legal requirement in examinations (Government of India 2016). Teachers who prepare learners for these tests are part of the system, and they have a voice within it.

items: Stakes map. A map of the tests learners take, with decisions and consequences noted for the highest-stakes tests.
Bias review. An item-by-item review of one paper with flagged items and proposed revisions.
Access analysis. An analysis of barriers to one high-stakes test for three learner profiles, with one school response.
Position statement. A short professional position on high-stakes testing, applied to a case.
Which test most shaped your own life? Was it a fair measure for the decision it informed?
Which of your learners are most disadvantaged by the tests they face?
Do your internal papers assume a single variety of English? Do they say so?
What accommodations have learners in your school received, and what have they missed?
How do you respond when parents ask about paid coaching?
Where in your sphere could you advocate for fairer assessment this year?

Screenshots of test providers’ websites or Google tools require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: A framework in which test developers must justify each link from a test performance to the interpretation of scores, the decisions made and their consequences for test takers (Bachman and Palmer 2010).
The aspect of validity concerned with the social consequences of test use, including its effects on teaching and learning (Messick 1989).
A situation in which a test item behaves differently for groups of equal ability, such as learners from different language backgrounds, suggesting possible bias.

Controlling access to education, jobs or migration through requirements such as English proficiency or high-stakes test scores. In India, English often acts as a gatekeeper to higher education and employment.
An assessment whose results have major consequences for the test-taker, such as admission, certification, employment or migration. Board examinations and international English tests are examples.
A change in how a test is given, such as extra time, large print, a reader or a separate room, that removes a barrier for a learner with a particular need without changing what the test measures.

Systematic unfairness in a test that disadvantages a group of test takers for reasons unrelated to the ability being measured, for example reading passages that assume familiarity with urban or foreign contexts.
The principle that a test gives all test takers an equal opportunity to show their ability, through unbiased content, appropriate accommodations, consistent administration and just use of scores.
Commercial coaching centres, books and courses that prepare candidates for high-stakes tests. It can help familiarity but raises fairness concerns, since access depends on ability to pay.
